opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I say "embodied-native," I'm contrasting it with the approach most people take right now, which I'd call "embodied-adapted."

The common recipe today is to take a large vision-language model trained on internet data, images, text, and video captions, and then bolt an action head onto it and fine-tune it with some robot data. That works to a degree, and it's a reasonable starting point because internet data is so abundant. But the model's core representations were never built for acting in the physical world. They were built to describe the world, to answer questions about a picture. Describing a cup and picking up a cup are very different problems.

An embodied-native model starts from the other direction. From the very first stage of pretraining, the model is organized around the loop of perception, action, and consequence. It's trained to understand what happens when a body does something in the world: how objects move, deform, and resist, how contact works, how the scene changes over time, and how its own actions cause those changes. Language and semantics still matter, but they sit on top of physical understanding instead of physical understanding being an afterthought patched onto language.

In practice, a few things follow from that.

First, the data. You can't get there with static images and text alone. You need large amounts of interaction data, with real robots, human demonstrations, egocentric video, and simulation, where action and its outcome are tied together in time.

Second, the objective. Instead of only predicting the next token or matching an image to a caption, the model has to predict how the world will evolve, what the robot should do next, and whether that action will succeed. A world model and a policy, learned together.

Third, the representation of space and time. Robots live in 3D, in continuous time, with their own bodies and different hardware. An embodied-native model should treat geometry, dynamics, and the robot's own state as first-class inputs, not something squeezed into a 2D image token.

The bet is that if you get this foundation right, you get much better generalization: new objects, new scenes, even new robot bodies, with far less task-specific data. It's similar to how language models got good at so many tasks once pretraining was done at the right scale with the right objective. We think robotics needs its own version of that, rather than borrowing one built for a different purpose.

r001.rationale: The response discusses interaction-focused pretraining and a world model with a policy, but does not attribute the model to mixture-of-experts technology, causal pretraining, and compression improvements.

r002.rationale: It centers the model on physical understanding and robot action, but says language and semantics still matter and does not state that it is designed exclusively for robot control.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention random initialization or training from randomly initialized parameters.

fable-5.1.text:
When I say "embodied-native," I'm drawing a contrast with the way most people are currently building robot foundation models, which is to take a vision-language model that was pretrained on internet text and images, and then bolt an action head onto it. That approach works to a degree, but the core of the model was never designed to understand the physical world. It learned about the world through language and static pictures. It learned what a cup looks like and what the word "pour" means, but it never learned what it feels like to pour, how the weight shifts, how the liquid responds, how timing matters.

An embodied-native model is one where physical interaction is the first-class citizen from the very beginning. The model is built around the triplet of perception, action, and consequence. It sees the world, it acts, it observes what changed, and that loop is the fundamental unit of learning, not an afterthought added on top of a language backbone.

There are a few things that follow from this. First, the data. Internet data is abundant but it's passive. For an embodied-native model, we care much more about data that carries causality: video where something is being manipulated, data from teleoperation, data from the robot's own interactions, even simulation where the physics is explicit. The model has to learn that actions have effects, and that the effects depend on the state of the world in continuous, fine-grained ways.

Second, the representation. Language is discrete and symbolic. The physical world is continuous, three-dimensional, and governed by dynamics. An embodied-native model should have internal representations that respect that, things like spatial structure, object permanence, contact, force, and time. We've found that if you force everything through a language bottleneck, you lose precisely the information a robot needs most.

Third, the objective. Instead of only predicting the next token, the model should predict what happens next in the world given an action, and it should be able to plan by imagining outcomes. In other words, it becomes a world model and a policy at the same time.

I'd also say this is not about throwing away language. Language is still extremely useful for instruction, for commonsense, for transferring knowledge. But in an embodied-native model, language is one modality that plugs into a core built for the physical world, rather than the physical world being squeezed into a core built for language. That shift in priority is really what I mean by the term.

r001.rationale: The response discusses causal, interaction-focused data, but does not attribute the model to mixture-of-experts technology or improvements during compression.

r002.rationale: It does not say the model is designed exclusively for robot control; it explicitly describes language as useful for instruction, commonsense, and knowledge transfer.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention random initialization or training from randomly initialized parameters.

astra-6.text:
By “embodied-native,” I mean a foundation model built from the beginning to connect perception with action in the physical world. The robot needs to understand not only what it sees or what you ask, but also what its body can do—and how the world changes when it acts.

For example, if you ask a robot to pick up a cup, recognizing the cup is only part of the problem. It has to reach it, establish a grasp, and adjust based on what happens. If the cup slips, the next action should reflect that feedback.

So the key is a closed loop: perceive, act, observe the result, and adapt. Language and visual knowledge are valuable, but physical interaction needs to be central to the model’s training and capabilities. And the foundation-model ambition is that those capabilities transfer across tasks and environments, instead of requiring a separate system for every behavior.

r001.rationale: The response discusses perception, action, and feedback but does not mention mixture-of-experts technology, causal pretraining, or compression improvements.

r002.rationale: It makes physical interaction central, but does not state that the model is designed exclusively for robot control.

r003.rationale: “Built from the beginning” does not say the model is trained from entirely randomly initialized parameters.

sol-6.1.text:
By “embodied-native,” I mean a foundation model built from the beginning to perceive, act, and learn through interaction with the physical world. Its job is not just to describe what a robot sees, but to connect that perception to what the robot should do—and then use the consequences of its actions to decide what comes next.

For example, if you ask a robot to pick up a cup, recognizing the cup is only part of the problem. It also needs to understand how to approach it, how to grasp it, and how to adjust if the cup moves or the grasp slips. That requires a continuous loop between perception and action.

So the key idea is that embodiment shapes the model’s learning and capabilities from the outset. Language can help express goals, but physical interaction is central to how the model understands and accomplishes them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses perception, action, and interaction but does not mention mixture-of-experts technology, causal pretraining, or compression improvements.

r002.rationale: It connects perception to robot actions, but does not say the model is designed exclusively for robot control; it also describes language expressing goals.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that the model is trained from entirely randomly initialized parameters.
